Shushi
Beyond Reach

Memory, Loss and Belonging

A personal and historical reflection on a city that can no longer be freely visited by Armenians, and on the photographs, cultural heritage and memories through which connection to place endures.

The central question
How do people remain connected to a place they can no longer physically return to?

Author’s note · Terminology

This project uses the Armenian name Shushi. In Azerbaijani, the city is called Shusha. I use Shushi because this story focuses on Armenian collective memory, cultural heritage, and my own relationship to the city; the terminology reflects that perspective.

Content note: This exhibition includes references to mass violence, forced displacement and the destruction of cultural heritage.

01

When an urban and cultural environment is disrupted

Shushi is physically inaccessible to Armenians today. This inaccessibility is not only about no longer being able to go there. With the loss of the city, the Armenian historical and cultural continuity formed in Shushi over centuries has been disrupted.

Some of the material layers that carried this continuity and memory have already been destroyed or altered, while others remain at risk.

This story is not an attempt to present the entire history of Shushi. It seeks to understand what happens to collective memory formed around a place when physical connection with that place is broken, while the material environment that carries that memory is destroyed or altered and its historical identity is distorted.

The rupture in Armenian presence and cultural continuity following the 2020 war had a historical precedent. A century earlier, the city had experienced a fundamental break in that continuity.

In the nineteenth century, Shushi developed into an important Armenian educational, intellectual, publishing and cultural centre. Schools, printing houses, bookshops and other institutions operated in the city. A printing house was established there at the end of 1827, and Armenian-language books were already being printed in 1828. In the following decades, Shushi’s publishing and educational life became an important part of its cultural environment.

One material witness to that world is the Shushi Real School, which opened in 1881 and operated until 1920. It was one of the key institutions in the city’s educational life. Many of its students went on to pursue higher education in Russia and Europe and became active in science, culture, professional fields, public life and politics.

The building of the Real School is therefore more than an old architectural structure. It is a material trace of an entire intellectual and social world.

A memorial plaque on a house in Shushi commemorates Martiros Sarukhanyan (1873–1896), who was born there and is identified on the plaque as one of the leaders of the 1896 Van self-defence.

In March 1920, the massacre of Shushi’s Armenian population and the burning of the Armenian part of the city destroyed not only residential neighbourhoods but also an established urban and cultural environment. Historian Gayane Makhmourian’s study, based on contemporary testimonies and extensive archival material, documents the massacre of civilians and the destruction of the Armenian part of the city.

1920 is not simply historical background here. It is a point of rupture in urban, cultural and social continuity.

02

1992: Return, victory and rebirth in Armenian public memory

This historical experience helps explain why, in 1992, Shushi acquired a meaning in Armenian collective memory that went far beyond its military significance.

In Armenian public memory, the events of May 1992 are remembered as the liberation of Shushi and as one of the key victories of the first war. In the following years, that victory became associated with return, reconstruction and cultural rebirth.

The Shushi Museum of History and Local Lore opened on 28 May 1992. In later years, museums, cultural institutions, exhibitions, educational programmes and public events in the city became part of its revived cultural life. The Shushi City History Museum collected and presented materials relating to the city’s architecture, public figures, everyday life and nineteenth-century cultural environment.

After 1992, rebirth was not only about constructing buildings or restoring monuments. It was also an attempt to reconnect with an interrupted historical continuity.

Together, the two images connect the memory of victory with the cultural and public life that continued after it.

Shushi thus became a symbol not only of victory, but also of return and rebirth after an earlier historical rupture.

03

2020: A new rupture

During the 2020 war, Azerbaijani forces took control of Shushi, and the city remained under Azerbaijani control following the 9 November ceasefire agreement.

In Armenian collective memory, the loss of Shushi carried significance beyond the loss of a single city. It disrupted a narrative that had developed over nearly three decades, in which Shushi had come to represent return, reconstruction and renewed urban life.

The loss of physical access was later accompanied by threats to the material foundations of memory.

In December 2021, the International Court of Justice ordered Azerbaijan to take all necessary measures to prevent and punish acts of vandalism and desecration affecting Armenian cultural heritage, including churches, places of worship, monuments, landmarks, cemeteries and cultural artefacts.

One of the most visible examples is the Church of St John the Baptist in Shushi, known as Kanach Zham. Eduard Minasyan photographed it in July 2016, when it was standing and restored. Satellite monitoring by Caucasus Heritage Watch documented that the church was completely destroyed between 28 December 2023 and 4 April 2024.

The same organisation has also documented the complete destruction of the old Armenian cemetery of Ghazanchetsots in Shushi. Monument Watch likewise documents the destruction and alteration of the city’s Armenian cultural heritage and what it describes as the reassignment of that heritage’s historical identity.

The rupture in the connection with Shushi is deeper than simply “you can no longer go there.” It is not only the territory that has become inaccessible. The material environment through which history and memory were preserved and transmitted is also being distorted or destroyed.

Curatorial note · Reading the photographs

The photographs in this exhibition document Shushi in 2016. They are evidence of places and buildings as they appeared before the 2020 war, not direct visual evidence of their current condition. Statements about subsequent damage or destruction are attributed to the court documents and heritage-monitoring organisations listed in Sources & Credits.

04

When the city remains in photographs

Physical inaccessibility does not mean the end of memory.

My photographs from Shushi are a simple example. They were taken at a time when I could enter the city, walk through its streets, visit its museums, see its historic buildings and experience its cultural life.

At the time, they were simply photographs taken during a visit. Today, their status has changed.

They have become a visual memory of an inaccessible environment. They preserve not only what a particular building looked like, but also the reality that these buildings were part of the everyday, cultural and historical environment of a living city.

Following the forced displacement of 2023, the digital environment has also become an important space for preserving the cultural memory of Artsakh. The “Artsakh Digital Cultural Home,” presented in 2026, was created to collect, preserve and make accessible elements of Artsakh’s intangible cultural heritage, including language, oral traditions, stories, rituals, music, crafts and other cultural layers.

The project is also connected to the reality that, after displacement, the natural transmission of cultural heritage within its spatial environment has been disrupted.

05

Beyond reach

The story of Shushi shows that the loss of a place can simultaneously be a territorial, material and mnemonic rupture.

In 1920, an already established Armenian urban, cultural and intellectual environment was disrupted. After 1992, the return of Shushi became associated in Armenian collective memory with victory and rebirth, as well as with the restoration of interrupted historical continuity. In 2020, that trajectory was disrupted again, while the loss of physical connection with the city was accompanied by threats to its Armenian material and cultural layers.

But Shushi does not disappear because it has become inaccessible.

It continues to exist in memory, photographs, stories, research and digital archives.

This is where Beyond Reach takes on its central meaning: a place may be beyond physical reach, but the question remains of how to preserve the historical, cultural and human connection with it when even the material foundations of that connection are at risk.

About the project

A story of memory and place

This exhibition is Lusine Mkhitaryan’s individual public-history project, first published on 18 September 2026.

The story

Across 1920, 1992, 2020 and the post-2023 displacement, Shushi becomes a way of thinking about the relationship between urban history, Armenian cultural heritage, collective memory and the possibility of remembering a place one can no longer reach.

Where and when?

Shushi (Shusha in Azerbaijani), in Nagorno-Karabakh/Artsakh. The narrative moves between the nineteenth century, the 1920 violence, the events of 1992, the 2020 war and the present.

Method and form

Digital exhibition / web story, developed as a solo project. The narrative draws on historical scholarship, cultural-heritage monitoring, institutional sources and photographs taken in 2016.
